content.text: Students draw on the comparisons, research notes, and myth patterns they developed across Lessons 22–39.
Myths across cultures explain danger, courage, transformation, and the unknown, and modern authors reshape those ideas for new audiences.
This lesson moves students from the essay outline they built in Lesson 39 into the drafting phase; in Lesson 41, students will deepen body paragraphs and integrate their visual evidence.
Students begin drafting Part 1: the Comparative Explanatory Essay by writing an introduction and body paragraph that explain a shared idea across
The Lightning Thief
and a myth from the unit. Students also continue planning Part 2: the Myth Comparison Visual so it clearly supports the essay’s main idea.
The Lightning Thief
by Rick Riordan
Selected myth texts or notes from prior lessons
Newsela Essay Outline from Lesson 39
Unit 4 Lesson 40 Student Edition
Performance Task Handout
Draft an explanatory introduction and body paragraph using evidence from myths across cultures.
Connect evidence to analysis by using precise academic verbs, varied sentence structures, and clear linking language.
Expand sentences with appositives and prepositional phrases to add clarity and style to essay drafts.
Students will draft an explanatory introduction and body paragraph using evidence from myths across cultures.
Students will connect evidence to analysis by using precise academic verbs, varied sentence structures, and clear linking language.
Students will expand sentences with appositives and prepositional phrases to add clarity and style to essay drafts.
Think-Pair-Share
Rehearse and Refine
Reflect and Response Dialogue
Turn and Talk
Think-Pair-Share

In Lesson 39, you already planned your Comparative Explanatory Essay by writing a thesis, organizing your evidence, and planning your visual. Today, you are not starting over; instead, you are turning that plan into clear, formal writing. Today, you will begin drafting Part 1 of the Performance Task by turning that outline into writing that sounds clear, precise, and ready for a reader. You will use the thesis you already wrote as the foundation for your introduction. You may revise wording as you draft, but your core idea should stay the same.
Access the Performance Task handout.
Directions:
Before you draft, reread Part 1 of the handout and notice what your essay must include: a clear thesis, evidence from both texts, explanation of what the texts reveal, and comparative transitions.
Write one strength and one drafting goal in your notes. Then, share with your partner and respond to the question.
Which part of your outline already feels ready to draft, and which part still needs work?
Sentence Expansion
Target Sentence:
“Luke looked furious, but he managed a sickly smile.”

This sentence from The Lightning Thief gives a strong story moment, but explanatory essays need writers to add context, analysis, and precision. When we draft today, we do not want our essay to sound choppy or vague. We are going to grow short ideas into stronger analytical sentences by adding information in smart places. A writer can do that with an appositive, which renames a noun, and a prepositional phrase, which adds location, time, or relationship.
Sentence Expansion for Analytical Writing
Directions:
Look at these sentence patterns and briefly learn how each works in essay writing.
Simple:
Myths warn people about danger.
Compound:
Myths warn people about danger, and they also teach cultural values.
Complex:
Although myths come from different cultures, they often reveal similar fears.
Why is the expanded sentence stronger for an essay than the short story sentence by itself?
Check for Understanding
Combine the shorter sentences into one analytical sentence: “Percy returns home. His choice reveals courage.” Use either an appositive or a prepositional phrase.
Part A: Draft an Introduction for the Comparative Explanatory Essay
Rehearse and Refine
Directions:

Look back at Part 1 of the Performance Task Handout. Your introduction should help you meet that part of the task by introducing the comparison clearly and ending with a thesis that explains a shared idea across texts. Open your essay outline from Lesson 39. You will use your planned myths, evidence, and existing thesis from Lesson 39 as the base for today’s introduction draft.

As you draft, build your introduction in this order: hook, context, connection, claim. In the margin, add one note about your Myth Comparison Visual and how it will help the reader better understand the shared idea in your essay.
How does the model introduction move from a broad idea to a focused claim?
What cultural value or human experience does your claim begin to explain?
Pulse Check
Which thesis would work best in an explanatory comparison essay?
Percy and Odysseus both return home after dangerous journeys, and both characters face many challenges along the way.
Although Percy and Odysseus both return home after difficult journeys, their stories show different ideas about responsibility and courage.
The Lightning Thief
and
The Odyssey
both include heroes, monsters, and long journeys.
Percy and Odysseus are both brave heroes who defeat many enemies.
Part B: Draft Body Paragraphs
Reflect and Response Dialogue
Directions:

Choose a point from your outline that directly supports your thesis. Your body paragraph should help prove the claim you already planned.Write a topic sentence, include evidence from your text, and add analysis that explains how the evidence supports your thesis and what it reveals about cultural values or human experiences. Then share either your introduction or your new body paragraph with a partner for feedback.
Where does the writing model connect evidence back to the thesis instead of only summarizing the story?
What is one helpful feedback statement you could give a partner after listening to a draft?

When you give feedback, say one strength and one revision step. Use one of these frames: I notice ___ is clear, but ___ could be expanded. This sentence connects evidence to analysis by ___. This detail still needs a sentence that explains ___.
Reflection
Reflect on your writing using the Reflection routine.
How clearly does your body paragraph explain your thesis, and which part of your paragraph—a topic sentence, your evidence, or your explanation—do you still want to improve?
Quick Write
Directions:

Reread Part 1 of the Performance Task Handout. Then reflect on which expectation your draft meets most clearly right now and which one still needs work. Use the following questions to guide your written response:
How well did your draft stay aligned to the thesis you wrote in Lesson 39, and which part of Part 1 of the handout still needs strengthening?
Which tool helped your draft most today—hook, context, connection, claim, sentence expansion, or precise verbs—and why did it help you meet the Performance Task more clearly?

Today you moved from the blueprint stage into real drafting. That matters because your performance task needs an introduction that guides the reader and body paragraphs that explain the evidence. The sentence work you practiced today will help you as you continue to write your essay in Lesson 41.
Think-Pair-Share
Have students take out their working essay outlines from Lesson 39 and the Performance Task Handout.
Say:
Before you draft, reread Part 1 of the handout and notice what your essay must include: a clear thesis, evidence from both texts, explanation of what the texts reveal, and comparative transitions.
Say these Directions:

In Lesson 39, you already planned your Comparative Explanatory Essay by writing a thesis, organizing your evidence, and planning your visual. Today, you are not starting over, instead you are turning that plan into clear, formal writing. Today, you will begin drafting Part 1 of the Performance Task by turning that outline into writing that sounds clear, precise, and ready for a reader. You will use the thesis you already wrote as the foundation for your introduction. You may revise wording as you draft, but your core idea should stay the same.
Write one strength and one drafting goal in your notes. Then, share with your partner and respond to the question.
Ask:
Which part of the Performance Task are you working on most today—your introduction, your explanation of evidence, or your visual connection?
I am mostly working on my introduction and making sure my claim is clear enough to guide the rest of the essay.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
You will now move from planning to drafting by learning how stronger sentences and more precise verbs can make your ideas sound clearer and more analytical.
Students access their Lesson 39 essay plans and begin drafting Part 1 of the Performance Task by turning their outline into clear, formal explanatory writing.
Sentence Expansion
Display the sentence and read it aloud.
Target Sentence:
“Luke looked furious, but he managed a sickly smile.”
Say:

This sentence from The Lightning Thief gives a strong story moment, but explanatory essays need writers to add context, analysis, and precision. When we draft today, we do not want our essay to sound choppy or vague. We are going to grow short ideas into stronger analytical sentences by adding information in smart places. A writer can do that with an appositive, which renames a noun, and a prepositional phrase, which adds location, time, or relationship.
Teach: Sentence Expansion for Analytical Writing
Say:
This sentence tells me what Luke does, but it does not yet explain why that moment matters. I can expand the noun with an appositive: “Luke,
Percy’s trusted friend,
” which helps my reader understand the relationship. I can add a prepositional phrase like a
t the end of the quest
or
behind a smile
to sharpen the image and the idea. Then I replace a vague verb like
shows
with a more precise verb like
reveals
or
emphasizes
. My expanded analytical sentence becomes: “In
The Lightning Thief
, Luke, Percy’s trusted friend, hides his anger behind a smile, which reveals that danger can grow inside a trusted community.”
Display these sentence patterns and briefly name how each works in essay writing:
Simple:
Myths warn people about danger.
Compound:
Myths warn people about danger, and they also teach cultural values.
Complex:
Although myths come from different cultures, they often reveal similar fears.
Ask:
Why is the expanded sentence stronger for an essay than the short story sentence by itself?

The expanded sentence is stronger because it gives context about who Luke is and explains the idea behind the moment. It also uses the verb reveals, which sounds more analytical than just says or shows.
Say:
When we expand sentences this way, we move from simply telling what happens in a story to explaining what the story means.
Check for Understanding (L.6.3.a)
Combine the shorter sentences into one analytical sentence: “Percy returns home. His choice reveals courage.” Use either an appositive or a prepositional phrase.
Connection to Today's Learning:
Say:
Now, you will use these sentence moves to draft introductions that do more than announce a topic; they begin to explain what the myths reveal.
Support students in expanding short idea units into clear analytical sentences that connect evidence to interpretation.
Language Focus:
Appositives that rename a noun
Prepositional phrases that add time, place, or relationship
Precise academic verbs such as reveals, emphasizes, implies, and suggests
Before Sentence Expansion (preparation step—optional)
Have students orally rehearse a kernel sentence and then add one detail aloud before writing it.
Prompt students to first name the main noun in the sentence and then decide what extra information the reader needs about it.
When students use vague verbs like shows or says, offer a short choice set of stronger verbs and ask which one best matches the idea.
You said “Percy is brave”—we can clarify that by saying “Percy’s choice reveals courage.“
That idea connects to interpretation because the writer is not only naming an event but also explaining what the event emphasizes.
In [text], ___, a/an ___, reveals ___.
Through ___, the myth emphasizes ___.
Although ___, the story suggests ___.
Allow students to rehearse the sentence first in a shared home language or in everyday English before reshaping it into formal academic English.
Affirm that students already know how to add detail in speech; the work today is transferring that skill into written academic language.
If a student adds detail that does not connect to the idea of the sentence → Prompt: “Add only the detail that helps your reader understand why this evidence matters.”
If a student writes two separate simple sentences instead of combining them → Prompt: “Try starting with Although, In, or Through to connect the ideas into one stronger sentence.”
Student combines two related ideas into one clearer sentence using an appositive, prepositional phrase, or subordinating word.
Student selects a precise verb that matches the claim instead of relying on vague verbs.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Expanding Sentences for Clarity

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Combining Ideas into One Sentence
Offer a frame such as: In [text], ___, a/an ___, reveals ___.
Struggling with: Choosing Precise Verbs
Display a small verb bank with reveals, emphasizes, suggests, and implies and have students test each verb aloud before writing.
Struggling with: Written Output
Allow students to say the sentence aloud to a partner or use speech-to-text before copying the final version into the journal.
Ready for extension

Revise one expanded sentence so it becomes complex instead of simple by adding although, because, or while. Ask students to write the same idea in two different sentence patterns and decide which version sounds stronger for an essay introduction.
Students learn how sentence expansion and precise verbs strengthen analytical writing.
Part A: Draft an Introduction for the Comparative Explanatory Essay (W.6.2.a) (15 minutes)
Rehearse and Refine
Have students get their working essay outline from Lesson 39 to use as the drafting guide for today’s introduction.
Say these Directions:

Look back at Part 1 of the Performance Task Handout. Your introduction should help you meet that part of the task by introducing the comparison clearly and ending with a thesis that explains a shared idea across texts. Open your essay outline from Lesson 39. You will use your planned myths, evidence, and existing thesis from Lesson 39 as the base for today’s introduction draft.
Display the following writing model for support and guidance:
Across many myths, dangerous journeys do more than entertain readers. They help cultures explain what courage looks like when the unknown feels overwhelming. In
The Lightning Thief
and
The Odyssey

, Percy and Odysseus both return home after major trials, but each story emphasizes a different kind of courage. Percy’s return highlights honesty and family responsibility, whereas Odysseus’s return highlights joy and gratitude. Together, these myths reveal that cultures admire bravery, but they do not always define it in the same way.
Teach: Building an Introduction from Hook to Claim
Say:

A strong introduction does four jobs in a small amount of space. It starts with a broad idea about myths, gives just enough context for the reader, connects that context to the exact texts or category, and ends with a claim that can guide the whole essay. I want my claim to sound precise, so I name both texts and the shared value they reveal. I also make sure the last sentence is specific enough that my body paragraph can prove it with evidence. As you draft, check that your final sentence matches your thesis from Lesson 39. If it changes, make sure it is a revision and not a completely new idea.
Say:

As you draft, build your introduction in this order: hook, context, connection, claim. In the margin, add one note about your Myth Comparison Visual and how it will help the reader better understand the shared idea in your essay.
Ask:
How does the model introduction move from a broad idea to a focused claim?

It begins with the big idea that myths explain courage. Then it names Percy and Odysseus, explains how both stories involve returning home, and ends with a clear claim about how each story defines courage differently.
Ask:
What cultural value or human experience does your claim begin to explain?
My claim begins to explain how different cultures connect courage to responsibility and belonging.
Say:

Rehearse your introduction aloud with your partner before you write it. Listen for whether the ending sentence sounds like a claim that can be proven with evidence. Then draft your full introduction in your journal.
Pulse Check (W.6.2.a, W.6.4)
Which thesis would work best in an explanatory comparison essay?
Percy and Odysseus both return home after dangerous journeys, and both characters face many challenges along the way.
Incorrect: This summarizes events but does not explain what idea the comparison reveals.
Although Percy and Odysseus both return home after difficult journeys, their stories show different ideas about responsibility and courage.
Correct: This thesis compares the texts and explains what idea the comparison reveals.
The Lightning Thief
and
The Odyssey
both include heroes, monsters, and long journeys.
Incorrect: This lists similarities but does not make an analytical claim.
Percy and Odysseus are both brave heroes who defeat many enemies.
Incorrect: This makes a general statement but does not explain what the comparison reveals about courage.
Support students in drafting introductions that move from a broad idea to a focused explanatory claim using precise, cohesive language.
Language Focus:
Introduction moves: hook, context, connection, claim
Comparative language such as both, whereas, unlike, across
Thesis language that names texts and a shared value or theme
Before Drafting (preparation step—optional)
Have students orally rehearse one sentence that names both myths and one sentence that states the shared value they reveal.
Remind students that a hook in explanatory writing should introduce an idea, not ask a random question or try to be dramatic.
If students are writing a classification essay, prompt them to name the myth category clearly in the claim rather than only listing titles.
You said “These myths are kind of about courage”—we can clarify that by saying “These myths reveal how different cultures define courage.”
That idea connects to your thesis because your introduction should move from the big pattern to the specific texts.
Across multiple myths, a recurring pattern emerges in which ___, revealing ___.
In [text 1] and [text 2], both authors explore ___, but ___ emphasizes ___ whereas ___ emphasizes ___.
This comparison suggests that cultures value ___, although they express that value in different ways.
Invite students to rehearse the thesis in everyday language first and then shift it into formal written English.
Honor students’ background knowledge of storytelling patterns by letting them name the pattern orally before turning it into a thesis statement.
If a student begins the introduction with a summary only → Prompt: “Start one step wider: what big ideas about myths or people are these texts helping you explain?”
If a student lists titles without a claim → Prompt: “After naming the texts, add what they reveal together about danger, courage, transformation, or the unknown.”
Student names the texts or category clearly and states a focused claim, not just a topic.
Student uses comparative or classificatory language to connect the texts to a shared cultural value.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Writing a Focused Claim
Give students a frame such as “In [text 1] and [text 2], both texts explore ___, but ___ reveals ___ whereas ___ reveals ___.”
Struggling with: Organizing the Introduction
Have students label their four sentences H, C, C, C for hook, context, connection, claim before revising into a smoother paragraph.
Struggling with: Written Output
Allow students to orally record their introduction first and then transcribe or use speech-to-text to capture it.
Ready for extension

Invite students to vary sentence openings so each sentence in the introduction begins differently. Challenge students to write an introduction that includes one complex sentence and one compound sentence while keeping the paragraph concise.
Part B: Draft Body Paragraphs (W.6.2.b) (15 minutes)
Reflect and Response Dialogue
Display the following writing model for support and guidance:
One way both stories connect courage to responsibility is through the hero’s return home. In
The Lightning Thief
, Percy chooses to go back to New York and face the truth about his family situation, which reveals that bravery can mean protecting people after the monster fight is over. In
The Odyssey

, when Odysseus finally sees his homeland, he kisses the ground and prays in gratitude,which shows how deeply he values returning safely to his home. Together, these details show that both heroes are brave, but each culture highlights a different responsibility connected to home.
Teach: Connecting Evidence to Analysis
Say:

A body paragraph needs more than a topic sentence and a detail from the text. After I include evidence, I need to explain what that detail reveals, emphasizes, or suggests about my claim. If I stop at summary, my reader has to do the thinking alone. Strong explanatory writing makes the connection visible.
Say these Directions:

Choose a point from your outline that directly supports your thesis. Your body paragraph should help prove the claim you already planned.Write a topic sentence, include evidence from your text, and add analysis that explains how the evidence supports your thesis and what it reveals about cultural values or human experiences. Then share either your introduction or your new body paragraph with a partner for feedback.
Ask:
Where does the writing model connect evidence back to the thesis instead of only summarizing the story?

The model connects back to the thesis when it says Percy’s choice reveals that bravery can mean protecting people after the fight is over. That sentence explains the meaning of the evidence instead of just retelling what happened.
Ask:
What is one helpful feedback statement you could give a partner after listening to a draft?
I notice your thesis is clear, but the sentence after your evidence could be expanded so the reader understands how that detail supports your idea about courage.
Say:

When you give feedback, say one strength and one revision step. Use one of these frames: I notice ___ is clear, but ___ could be expanded. This sentence connects evidence to analysis by ___. This detail still needs a sentence that explains ___.
Reflection (W.6.5)
Reflect on your writing using the
Reflection
routine.

How clearly does your body paragraph explain your thesis and show what the text reveals, and which part of your paragraph—a topic sentence, your evidence, or your explanation—do you still want to improve?
Support students in developing body paragraphs that connect evidence to analysis and in giving constructive peer feedback with clear, specific language.
Language Focus:
Evidence-to-analysis moves using because, which reveals, which emphasizes, and this suggests
Precise academic verbs to explain how evidence supports a claim
Feedback language that identifies one clear strength and one revision need
Before Drafting (preparation step—optional)
Have students underline one point from their outline that will become today’s body paragraph focus.
If students begin stacking evidence without explanation, stop them after each detail and ask what the evidence reveals about the claim.
Keep peer feedback grounded in the writing, not the writer, by asking students to comment on clarity, connection, and cohesion.
You said, “This quote shows courage”—we can explain that by saying “This detail reveals how the hero accepts responsibility under pressure.”
You said, “Make this part better”—we can give clearer feedback by saying “This sentence could be expanded to connect the evidence back to the thesis.”
This detail reveals ___ because ___.
The evidence from
The Lightning Thief
emphasizes ___, which connects to the thesis by ___.
I notice ___ is clear, but ___ could be expanded so the reader understands ___.
Allow partners to discuss their evidence in a home language or in mixed language first and then restate the strongest idea in academic English for the draft.
Recognize that strong oral explanation is a resource; invite students to speak the explanation before writing it.
If a student copies evidence into the draft without explanation → Prompt: “Finish this sentence: This detail matters because ___.”
If a student gives vague peer feedback such as “It is good” → Prompt: “Name the exact sentence and tell what it does well or what it still needs.”
Student uses evidence and follows it with analysis that links back to the thesis or category.
Student gives partner feedback that names a specific sentence-level strength or revision need.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Drafting an Essay Paragraph

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Connecting Evidence to Analysis
Offer a quick scaffold: “This detail matters because ___. This reveals ___ about ___.”
Struggling with: Starting the Body Paragraph
Provide a topic sentence frame such as: “One way these myths reveal ___ is through ___.”
Struggling with: Peer Feedback Language
Give students two required stems to choose from so feedback stays specific and kind.
Struggling with: Written Output
Allow students to record their paragraph explanation orally before writing or to use speech-to-text for the first draft.
Ready for extension

Challenge students to integrate evidence from two myths in the same paragraph with a smooth transition such as similarly, however, or unlike. Invite students to revise one paragraph sentence for stronger rhythm by changing a repeated sentence opening or mixing simple and complex structures.

Part A: Draft an Introduction for the Comparative Explanatory Essay (W.6.2.a) Learning in Action B: Draft Body Paragraphs (W.6.2.b) Students will begin a body paragraph by integrating evidence and analysis, then use peer feedback to strengthen clarity and cohesion.

Students will draft an introduction that includes a hook, context, connection, and claim while noting a possible supporting visual. Learning in Action B: Draft Body Paragraphs (W.6.2.b) Students will begin a body paragraph by integrating evidence and analysis, then use peer feedback to strengthen clarity and cohesion.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Reread Part 1 of the Performance Task Handout. Then reflect on which expectation your draft meets most clearly right now and which one still needs work.
Ask:
How well did your draft stay aligned to the thesis you wrote in Lesson 39, and which part of Part 1 of the handout still needs strengthening?

My draft stays aligned to my thesis because my claim clearly explains a shared idea across both texts. I still need to strengthen how I explain what my evidence reveals about cultural values or human experiences.
Ask:
Which tool helped your draft most today—hook, context, connection, claim, sentence expansion, or precise verbs—and why did it help you meet the Performance Task more clearly?
Sentence expansion helped me the most because it stopped my writing from sounding choppy. When I added an appositive and used emphasizes instead of shows, my paragraph sounded more like an essay.
Say:

Today you moved from the blueprint stage into real drafting. That matters because your performance task needs an introduction that guides the reader and body paragraphs that explain evidence, not just list it. The sentence work you practiced today will help you as you continue to write your essay in Lesson 41.
Optional Sentence Starter:
The tool that helped me most was ___ because ___.
Students will reflect on one sentence-level craft move they used today and name a next step for continuing the draft.
Instruct students to continue their draft.
Use today’s peer feedback and your outline to finish your introduction, add more to your first body paragraph, and keep revising your visual plan so it matches your shared idea.

data.subject: ELA

standards.description: Vary sentence patterns for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.

Introduce a topic or thesis statement; organize ideas, concepts, and information, using strategies such as definition, classification, comparison/contrast, and cause/effect; include formatting (e.g., headings), graphics (e.g., charts, tables), and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.
Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

Write longer and more detailed literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently using appropriate text organization and growing understanding of register.
Write short literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently.
Write longer literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently using appropriate text organization.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with light support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with substantial support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with moderate support.

Expand noun phrases in an increasing variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative and general academic adjectives to noun phrases or more complex clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
Expand noun phrases in simple ways (e.g., adding a sensory adjective to a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.

Expand noun phrases in a variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative adjectives to noun phrases or simple clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.

How do stories from different cultures explore danger, courage, or the unknown?
